In such places as Abel Tasman,

It's about our relationship and connection to place and to

trust that has existed since 1845 but
was not properly recognized or managed by the Crown.
And so our tupuna have never given up on that promise,

Taonga data or artificial intelligence.
My professional work focuses on governance systems, and regardless of

Who has legitimate authority to decide?
To me, this bill begins to answer that question.
One of the strengths of this legislation is that it does not present
Māori authority and public administration as opposing
concepts. Instead, it creates a practical governance model where
both have a role to play. The Department of Conservation, local
authorities, and other public agencies will continue to have important
statutory responsibilities. At the same time, Te Henui
Anuku Trust will hold the legal authority of the
trustee on behalf of the beneficial owners.
That shouldn't be seen as a source of concern.
It should be recognized as an opportunity to strengthen governance.
For generations, Māori have exercised stewardship of these lands and waters
through whakapapa, tikanga, and intergenerational knowledge.
That knowledge has sustained these spaces long before modern
government agencies existed. Bringing that knowledge
together with the statutory responsibility of public institutions
creates a stronger foundation for decision-making
rather than the being able to make them
alone. Good governance is not about replacing one system with
another. It is about ensuring that every organization exercises
its responsibility within the limits of its
legitimate authority while working together in the interests of
both the whenua and the wider public,
which is also consistent with our constitutional foundations.
Article 2 of Te Tiriti o Waitangi guarantees the continued
exercise of tino rangatiratanga over lands, kaimoana, and
taonga. While this bill cannot undo generations of loss,
it recognizes that the authority over the whenua should sit with those
who hold enduring whakapapa connections to it.
It is equally consistent with the United Nations Declarations on the Rights of
Indigenous Peoples, which recognizes, of course, the rights of Indigenous

territories, and resources and to maintain-
